title: Design an In-Memory Multi-Core OLTP Index Engine with Adaptive Radix Trees & Epoch Reclamation
tagline: Sustaining 20M+ concurrent reads and writes/sec on 64 cores with OLC, EBR, and zero reader cache-line bouncing.
purpose: Design a thread-safe, memory-bounded ordered index engine for an in-memory OLTP database that supports point lookups, range scans, and concurrent node resizing without use-after-free bugs.
prompt: Design an in-memory ordered index engine for a 64-core OLTP database holding 500M keys (mixed 64-bit IDs and variable-length composite keys) with 90% point/range reads and 10% inserts/deletes, targeting <500 ns p99 lookup latency and zero use-after-free crashes during node grow/shrink.

prerequisites.title: Adaptive Radix Trees (ART)
prerequisites.summary: Know Node4/16/48/256 layouts, path compression, and why OLC uses version counters instead of reader locks.

prerequisites.title: Memory Reclamation (EBR / Hazard Pointers)
prerequisites.summary: Understand why lock-free/optimistic readers cannot allow writers to `free()` a replaced node immediately.

spark.summary: Pair ART (Node4/16/48/256) with Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC) for zero-write read paths and Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) with bounded limbo-list reclamation.
spark.keyTakeaway: When building a multi-core in-memory OLTP index, combine Adaptive Radix Trees with Optimistic Lock Coupling for lock-free reads and Epoch-Based Reclamation so node grow/shrink never triggers use-after-free crashes.
spark.byteSummary:
An in-memory OLTP engine serving 500M keys across 64 cores will collapse if readers acquire shared mutexes or RW-locks—every atomic lock increment bounces the cache line across all 64 cores. Yet simply removing locks causes readers to crash with use-after-free segfaults whenever a writer grows a Node4 into a Node16 and frees the old Node4.

The architecture pairs an Adaptive Radix Tree (ART) with Optimistic Lock Coupling (OLC) and Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR). Readers enter a thread-local epoch guard (`epoch_enter()`), traverse nodes by validating monotonic 64-bit version counters before and after reading child pointers, and restart if a writer bumped a node's version or set its obsolete bit.

Writers acquire per-node exclusive write locks in top-down coupling order, allocate the new Node16/48/256, atomically swap the parent's child pointer, mark the old node obsolete, and push it onto a thread-local EBR limbo list. A background or amortized reclamation sweep frees retired nodes only after all active worker threads have exited older epochs—while a quiescent watchdog ensures stalled threads cannot pin memory indefinitely.

learningJourney.title: R & E · Requirements, Memory Budget & Latency Math
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Establishes exact DRAM bounds for 500M keys and why cache misses dominate the 500 ns budget.

explanation.foundation: With 500M keys and a 500 ns p99 lookup budget, you can afford at most 4–5 DRAM cache misses (~70–90 ns each) per lookup—leaving zero room for lock contention.
explanation.core: Illustrative Memory Sizing: At ~48–60 bytes per key including inner nodes + 8-byte leaf pointers, 500M keys occupy ~24–30 GB of DRAM for inner structure plus leaf payloads—easily fitting inside a single 256 GB–512 GB dual-socket server, compared to ~100+ GB for a naive 256-way trie.
explanation.deepDive: If a reader acquires a standard `std::shared_mutex` on the root node, 64 cores contending on that single cache line serialize throughput below 2M ops/sec. Write-free OLC version reads eliminate all inter-core invalidations on the read path, scaling linearly past 20M+ ops/sec.

learningJourney.title: S · Storage & Cache-Aligned Node Headers
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Embeds the OLC version word, obsolete bit, and compressed prefix into a single cache line.

explanation.foundation: Every ART inner node starts with a compact 16-byte header so the CPU fetches the version word, node type, and compressed prefix in the exact same 64-byte cache line.
explanation.core: Header layout: `uint64_t version_lock_obsolete` (8B: bit 0 = lock, bit 1 = obsolete, bits 2..63 = monotonic version), `uint8_t type` (Node4/16/48/256), `uint8_t count`, `uint16_t prefix_len`, and `uint8_t prefix[8]` (8B inline compressed prefix). Total header = 20 bytes.
explanation.deepDive: For Node4 (20B header + 4B keys + 32B pointers = 56 bytes), the entire node fits inside a single 64-byte CPU cache line! A reader loads the header and all 4 children in one memory fetch.

learningJourney.title: H & A · High-Level Engine & OLC Traversal Contract
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Defines the exact read/validate/restart contract and range-scan cursor semantics.

explanation.foundation: Every lookup or range scan begins by registering the worker thread's current epoch (`EbrGuard`) and reading the root node's version.
explanation.core: During traversal, before dereferencing `child = parent.find_child(byte)`, the reader checks `parent.read_unlock_or_restart(v_parent)`. Only after confirming `parent` was untouched does it load `v_child` and descend—this is 'lock coupling' without holding any read locks!
explanation.deepDive: For range scans (`scan(low, high)`), OLC validates each node along the DFS stack; if any node version changes mid-scan, the iterator restarts from the last validated key (`last_key`) rather than from `low`, guaranteeing forward progress even under concurrent writes.

learningJourney.title: D · Detailed Design: Node Grow/Shrink & Epoch Reclamation
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents use-after-free crashes when writers replace Node4->Node16 under concurrent readers.

explanation.foundation: A writer cannot call `delete old_node` immediately after swapping a Node4 for a Node16, because an optimistic reader might still be inspecting `old_node` before its validation check.
explanation.core: With 3-epoch EBR (`e`, `e-1`, `e-2`), each worker keeps a local limbo list of retired nodes tagged with the epoch `e` when they were retired. Periodically, a thread scans all active threads' announced epochs; once `min_active_epoch >= e + 2`, every node retired in epoch `e` is guaranteed unreachable by any reader and is freed in batch.
explanation.deepDive: If a Node48 shrinks below 13 children (hysteresis threshold < 16 to avoid thrashing!), the writer allocates a Node16, swaps the parent pointer, marks the Node48 obsolete (`version |= OBSOLETE_BIT`), and retires it to EBR. Hysteresis (grow at 16, shrink at 12) prevents repeated alloc/free ping-pong on oscillating workloads.

decisionFramework.problem: How to safely reclaim retired ART nodes without slowing down optimistic readers.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Immediately `free()` replaced nodes or use per-pointer Hazard Pointers on every hop.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Immediate `free()` causes segfaults on concurrent OLC readers; Hazard Pointers require an expensive atomic store + memory fence (`MFENCE`) at every single tree level.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Reference counting vs. Hazard Pointers vs. 3-Epoch Based Reclamation (EBR).
decisionFramework.decision: Use 3-Epoch Based Reclamation (EBR) with hysteresis on node shrink and a bounded-epoch stall check.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Amortizes reclamation overhead to once per operation batch (zero fences inside tree traversal), assuming workers do not block inside an epoch guard.

decisionExercise.prompt: During a bulk delete workload, a worker thread enters an EBR epoch guard, then makes a slow synchronous HTTP call to an external service before exiting the guard. What happens to the 64-core OLTP index?

options.label: The stalled thread pins the minimum active epoch, preventing all 64 cores from freeing retired nodes in EBR limbo lists and causing unbounded memory growth.
options.explanation: Correct! EBR can only free nodes older than the earliest active reader epoch. Never perform blocking I/O inside an EBR guard; keep guards strictly scoped to in-memory index operations.

options.label: Other threads automatically switch from ART to a B+Tree.
options.explanation: Threads continue using ART; only memory reclamation stalls.

options.label: EBR immediately frees the nodes anyway after 10 ms.
options.explanation: Freeing while a thread holds an old epoch would violate memory safety and risk use-after-free.

learningJourney.title: E & D · Evaluation, Assumptions, Limitations & Glossary
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Documents hardware assumptions, stalled-epoch risks, and core concurrency terms.

explanation.foundation: This design assumes all index data fits in DRAM on a cache-coherent NUMA server and that threads exit EBR guards within microseconds.
explanation.core: Assumptions & Limitations: Memory estimates (~24–30 GB for 500M keys) assume moderate key prefix sharing and exclude WAL/MVCC tuple payloads. Under extreme skew where 64 writers continuously resize the exact same Node4/Node16, OLC read restarts can spike; falling back to a brief shared read lock after K=8 restarts guarantees bounded tail latency.
explanation.deepDive: Glossary: OLC (Optimistic Lock Coupling — version-validated lock-free reads + exclusive write locks); EBR (Epoch-Based Reclamation — deferred batch freeing across 3 global epochs); Limbo List (Per-thread queue of retired pointers awaiting epoch advancement); Hysteresis (Gap between grow and shrink thresholds to prevent node thrashing).

steps.title: Write-Free OLC Point & Range Reads
steps.explanation: 64 cores traverse Node4/16/48/256 in parallel without writing any lock words, sustaining 22M ops/sec.

steps.title: Writer Promotes Node16 -> Node48
steps.explanation: Writer locks parent and child, allocates Node48, swaps the pointer, and marks the old Node16 obsolete.

steps.title: Optimistic Reader Restarts Safely
steps.explanation: An in-flight reader sees OBSOLETE_BIT set during validation and cleanly restarts; old Node16 stays valid in EBR limbo.

steps.title: Epoch 44 Advances & Reclaims Memory
steps.explanation: Once all readers pass epoch 43, EBR batch-frees all retired nodes from epoch 42.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does an OLC-based ART engine use a shrink hysteresis threshold (e.g., grow Node16->48 at 17 keys, shrink Node48->16 at 12 keys)?

options.text: To prevent repeated node allocations and EBR retirements when inserts/deletes oscillate right around 16 keys.
options.feedback: Correct! Without hysteresis, alternating insert/delete at the boundary thrashes allocators and floods EBR limbo lists.

options.text: Because Node48 cannot hold fewer than 12 pointers in C++.
options.feedback: Node48 can physically hold any count <= 48; hysteresis is purely for stability.

options.text: To keep the OLC version counter even.
options.feedback: Version parity only tracks whether a write lock is currently held.

options.text: Because SIMD instructions only work on multiples of 12.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Hysteresis avoids pathological allocation/reclamation thrashing at node size boundaries.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is Epoch-Based Reclamation (EBR) preferred over Hazard Pointers on every ART node traversal?

options.text: Hazard Pointers require an expensive atomic store + memory barrier on every node hop, whereas EBR only updates an epoch once per operation.
options.feedback: Correct! Per-hop fences would destroy ART's <500 ns read latency budget.
Hazard Pointers work on any pointer size, just with higher per-hop overhead.

options.text: EBR works even if a reader thread hangs indefinitely inside an epoch.
options.feedback: That is actually Hazard Pointers' advantage—EBR requires threads to exit guards promptly.

options.text: EBR eliminates the need for OLC version validation.
options.feedback: EBR protects memory lifetime; OLC protects logical read consistency.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Amortizing memory safety to one epoch entry/exit per query preserves ART's cache-line efficiency.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if an OLC reader experiences repeated restarts (e.g., >8 retries) on a heavily contended node?

options.text: Fallback to acquiring a brief shared/exclusive lock or bounded backoff so tail latency stays bounded without starvation.
options.feedback: Correct! Bounded optimistic retries + lock fallback prevents livelock under extreme write hotspots.

options.text: Return stale data without validating the version.
options.feedback: Returning unvalidated data can read torn pointers or corrupted keys.

options.text: Force an immediate EBR global reclamation.
options.feedback: EBR reclamation does not resolve write contention on a live node.
Deleting live index nodes would cause data loss.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Hybrid optimistic-then-pessimistic fallback guarantees forward progress under extreme hotspot writes.

beginner.summary: Build a fast multi-core in-memory index by letting readers check node versions without locks and freeing replaced nodes safely via epochs.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When 64 CPU cores read an in-memory index at once, avoid reader locks by checking node version numbers and delaying node deletion until active readers finish.
beginner.byteSummary: Instead of slowing down 64 cores with reader locks, readers check a node's version number before and after reading. When a writer resizes a node, Epoch-Based Reclamation waits until all active readers move on before freeing the old memory.

intermediate.summary: Combine ART (Node4/16/48/256) with OLC version validation and 3-epoch EBR limbo lists to achieve <500 ns p99 lookups across 64 cores.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When designing a multi-core OLTP index, pair ART + OLC with 3-epoch EBR and shrink hysteresis to prevent cache-line bouncing and allocator thrashing.
intermediate.byteSummary: Embedding a 64-bit OLC version word in ART's 20-byte header keeps reads write-free, while 3-epoch EBR safely frees obsolete nodes after grow/shrink without per-hop memory fences.

advanced.summary: Cache-line-aligned ART headers with OLC, 3-epoch EBR with shrink hysteresis, and retry-bounded pessimistic fallback for hotspot keys.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When targeting 20M+ ops/sec on 64 cores with <500 ns p99, keep EBR guards strictly scoped off I/O and add bounded-retry fallback for hotspot nodes.
advanced.byteSummary: Packing OLC version/lock/obsolete bits + 8B inline prefix into one 64B cache line, pairing 3-epoch EBR with grow/shrink hysteresis, and capping OLC restarts with lock fallback delivers predictable <500 ns p99 under skew.
